meta.cohort_policy: Latest submission cohort per experiment/platform, including failed latest attempts; no pooling across config/runtime identities.

studies.title: S1 · Gradient accumulation
studies.question: If each GPU does several micro-batches before the gradients are exchanged, does scaling efficiency recover?
studies.plain: Every training step ends with all GPUs swapping their gradients. Accumulation lets each GPU do 2, 4 or 8 small steps before that swap, so the swap is paid less often. If a slow link is the bottleneck, this should help most where the link is slowest.
design: Fixed micro-batch per workload: GPT-2 8×1024, DistilBERT 32×512, TinyLlama 4×1024 (sequences × tokens).
Accumulation 1/2/4/8 at 1/2/4/8 GPUs on L40S; accumulation 1 and 4 at 1/2/4 GPUs on H100 (compact block).
Efficiency = throughput at N GPUs ÷ (N × throughput of the matched 1-GPU run, same accumulation, same runtime cohort).
findings: H100 TinyLlama-1.1B at 4 GPUs: efficiency 90% with no accumulation → 96% with accumulation 4 (throughput +22.6%, CI +22.3% to +23.0%).
H100 GPT-2 Small at 4 GPUs: efficiency 96% with no accumulation → 99% with accumulation 4 (throughput +6.0%, CI +5.7% to +6.2%).
H100 DistilBERT at 4 GPUs: efficiency 92% with no accumulation → 97% with accumulation 4 (throughput +12.3%, CI +11.7% to +12.9%).
L40S TinyLlama-1.1B at 8 GPUs: efficiency 54% with no accumulation → 87% with accumulation 8 (throughput +117.2%, CI +117.0% to +117.4%).
L40S GPT-2 Small at 8 GPUs: efficiency 88% with no accumulation → 97% with accumulation 8 (throughput +17.2%, CI +16.9% to +17.4%).
L40S DistilBERT at 8 GPUs: efficiency 80% with no accumulation → 95% with accumulation 8 (throughput +33.8%, CI +33.5% to +34.1%).

Across all 45 matched contrasts accumulation never hurt throughput (44 helps, 1 inconclusive, 0 hurts). The gain grows with GPU count and model size, which is what a gradient-exchange bottleneck predicts.
caveats: Accumulation changes the global batch, so these are system-throughput results, not time-to-accuracy results.
H100 ran a compact block (accumulation 1 and 4 only, up to 4 GPUs); compare platforms at matching settings only.

studies.title: S2 · Batch × sequence split
studies.question: At the same number of tokens per GPU, does it matter whether they arrive as many short sequences or a few long ones?
studies.plain: Each GPU processes the same amount of text per step, but split differently: 32 sequences of 256 tokens versus 8 of 1,024, for example. Attention cost grows faster than linearly with sequence length, so the split could change both speed and scaling.
design: Two token budgets per workload (GPT-2 8,192 and 2,048; DistilBERT 8,192 and 2,048; TinyLlama 4,096 and 2,048 tokens per GPU per micro-step).
Three splits per budget, 1/2/4/8 GPUs. The control is the longest-sequence split of each budget.
L40S has the full grid; H100 has only shared controls so far.
findings: DistilBERT is insensitive to the split: all 16 contrasts are within ±1.8%.

TinyLlama's single-GPU benefit from shorter sequences disappears at 8 GPUs (16×256 +1.8%, 4×512 +0.6%, 8×256 +0.9%, 8×512 +1.3%): once communication dominates, how the tokens are shaped stops mattering.
Rule of thumb supported: tokens per GPU per step, not the batch/sequence split, is what governs scaling efficiency.
caveats: Two H100 contrasts in the export compare 8×1024 with 8×1024. They are the run-length check (1,000 vs 200 updates), not a split, and are excluded here (see Run length).

studies.title: S3 · Model size and gradient volume
studies.question: At the same work per GPU, how does scaling efficiency change as the model gets bigger?
studies.plain: A bigger model has more gradients to exchange after every step, but each GPU's compute per step also grows. This study holds the work per GPU fixed (4 sequences × 512 tokens) and changes only the model, from 66M to 1.1B parameters.
design: Models: DistilBERT 66M, GPT-2 Small 124M, GPT-2 Medium 355M, GPT-2 Large 774M, TinyLlama 1.1B.
4×512 per GPU, accumulation 1 and 4, 1/2/4/8 GPUs (L40S). H100 has not run this block yet.
findings: Without accumulation, 8-GPU L40S efficiency: DistilBERT 40%, GPT-2 Small 58%, GPT-2 Medium 51%, GPT-2 Large 50%, TinyLlama-1.1B 41%. Within the GPT-2 family it falls as the model grows; DistilBERT and TinyLlama are lowest, so size alone does not predict it — work per step relative to gradient volume does (DistilBERT does very little compute per step at this shape).
Accumulation 4 at the same micro-batch: DistilBERT 62%, GPT-2 Small 81%, GPT-2 Medium 76%, GPT-2 Large 76%, TinyLlama-1.1B 64%.
Efficiency gained from accumulation 4: DistilBERT +21 pts, GPT-2 Small +23 pts, GPT-2 Medium +24 pts, GPT-2 Large +25 pts, TinyLlama-1.1B +23 pts — a similar gain for every model at this small shape.
caveats: 4×512 is small work per GPU by design, so absolute efficiencies here are lower than in S1's larger shapes.

studies.title: S4 · DDP communication settings
studies.question: Which DDP settings recover efficiency on PCIe, and do they matter on NVLink?
studies.plain: PyTorch DDP sends gradients in 'buckets' while the backward pass is still running. Bucket size changes how well sending overlaps computing; BF16 compression halves the bytes sent. These are one-line settings, so a clear win would be cheap to adopt.
design: Settings: 5 MB and 100 MB buckets (default 25 MB), BF16 gradient compression, compression + 100 MB, bucket view + static graph.
Primary shapes (GPT-2 8×1024, DistilBERT 32×512, TinyLlama 4×1024), accumulation 1, 2/4/8 GPUs.
Control: default DDP at the same GPU count.
findings: L40S TinyLlama-1.1B at 8 GPUs: best setting 100 MB + BF16 compression +33.7% (helps); worst 5 MB buckets -0.1% (no material effect).
H100 TinyLlama-1.1B at 4 GPUs: best setting 100 MB buckets +0.8% (no material effect); worst BF16 compression -4.6% (hurts).
L40S GPT-2 Small at 8 GPUs: best setting BF16 compression +4.4% (helps); worst 100 MB buckets -3.3% (hurts).
L40S DistilBERT at 8 GPUs: best setting BF16 compression +6.9% (helps); worst 100 MB buckets -7.1% (hurts).
Pattern: compression pays where the link is the bottleneck (large model on PCIe) and costs a little where it isn't (NVLink); bucket size and static graph are second-order.
caveats: H100 has TinyLlama only (2 and 4 GPUs).

studies.title: S5 · Training stacks: DDP versus FSDP
studies.question: Does sharding the model (FSDP) scale better or worse than replicating it (DDP), with identical inputs?
studies.plain: DDP keeps a full copy of the model on every GPU and exchanges gradients. FSDP splits the model's state across GPUs, which changes what is sent and when: more, smaller messages that can overlap computation. Wrapping each layer separately ('per-layer') or the whole model ('root') changes that overlap again.
design: FSDP sharded_grad_op (per-layer wrap), full_shard (per-layer wrap), full_shard (root wrap) versus DDP.
Primary shapes, accumulation 1, 2/4/8 GPUs. Plus TinyLlama 8×1024 under FSDP, a shape DDP cannot fit on L40S.
findings: L40S TinyLlama at 8 GPUs: FSDP grad-op shard (per-layer) +113.6% over DDP (CI +113.2% to +114.1%).
H100 TinyLlama at 4 GPUs: FSDP full shard (root wrap) +34.3% over DDP (CI +33.5% to +35.1%).
Wrapping matters: for DistilBERT on L40S, root-wrapped full_shard 2 GPU +2.5%, 4 GPU -19.0%, 8 GPU -23.0%; per-layer wrapping helps at 8 GPUs (see matched contrasts below).
On L40S at 8 GPUs, per-layer FSDP beats DDP in all 6 contrasts (+5% to +114%); the gap grows with model size.

studies.title: S6 · GPU placement, peer-to-peer and NCCL algorithm
studies.question: Does it matter which L40S GPUs a job lands on, or how NCCL moves the data?
studies.plain: On the L40S node, GPUs come in pairs that share a PCIe switch; other pairs talk through the CPU interconnect, and half the GPUs sit on a second CPU socket. If placement mattered, unpinned jobs would vary from run to run depending on where Slurm put them.
design: Pinned GPU sets: same PCIe switch (0,1), same socket (0,2), across sockets (0,4); 4-GPU sets 0-3, 0,1,4,5 and 0,2,4,6.
P2P disabled; NCCL Ring vs Tree. Original deep-dive runs E608–E637 compare with unpinned default runs.

Recovery set E796–E809 re-ran the interrupted conditions in one current runtime cohort with matched defaults (E796 GPT-2, E806 TinyLlama). Its Tree/Ring settings apply to all-reduce only (allreduce:Tree), replacing the original invalid global Tree setting (E617 failed).
findings: Original contrasts: 13 of 14 show no material effect — pinning to a shared PCIe switch, a single socket, or across sockets changed GPT-2 and TinyLlama throughput by under 3% at 2 and 4 GPUs.

Recovery set material effects: TinyLlama-1.1B 4 GPU GPUs 0,1,4,5 -5.2%; TinyLlama-1.1B 4 GPU GPUs 0,2,4,6 -3.3%; TinyLlama-1.1B 2 GPU GPUs 0,4, P2P off -4.8%; TinyLlama-1.1B 8 GPU allreduce:Tree -12.1%.

Placement and NCCL effects are at most a few percent (all-reduce Tree is the exception at −12%), an order of magnitude smaller than the +33% to +117% from compression, FSDP and accumulation (S1, S4, S5). Placement does not explain the earlier poor TinyLlama scaling on L40S.
caveats: Topology is the one captured by E215 on this node: switch pairs (0,1), (2,3), (4,5), (6,7); GPUs 4–7 on socket 1.

studies.title: S7 · Real text: padding, packing and stragglers
studies.question: Do realistic variable-length inputs cost speed or scaling that synthetic fixed-length data hides?
studies.plain: Real paragraphs are short and uneven. Padding every one to 1,024 tokens wastes compute; padding each batch only to its own longest item wastes less but makes GPUs finish at different times; packing joins paragraphs into full windows and wastes nothing. Throughput here counts only real (non-padding) tokens.
design: WikiText-103 (pinned revision), GPT-2 8×1024 and TinyLlama 4×1024, 1/2/4/8 GPUs on L40S.
Modes: pad to max, dynamic padding, length-bucketed dynamic padding, packing. Control: pad to max.
findings: GPT-2 Small, 8 GPUs: packing delivers 7.9× the useful tokens/s of pad-to-max (padding 86% vs 0%); dynamic padding 2.1×, rank imbalance 1.43.
TinyLlama-1.1B, 8 GPUs: packing delivers 6.4× the useful tokens/s of pad-to-max (padding 84% vs 0%); dynamic padding 1.2×, rank imbalance 1.52.
Bucketing reduces padding relative to dynamic padding but the gain over dynamic padding is small and, for TinyLlama at 2 GPUs, inconclusive.
caveats: TinyLlama-1.1B at 2 GPUs is slower than at 1 GPU in 2 of 4 modes (length-bucketed, pack), the same 2-GPU L40S anomaly first seen in E291; its 2-GPU points are shown but should not be read as a scaling trend.
Large percentages are real but reflect the metric: pad-to-max at 1,024 tokens processes mostly padding for short WikiText paragraphs.

studies.title: S8 · Numeric precision under scaling
studies.question: Does faster arithmetic (BF16, FP8) leave communication more exposed, and how much speed does each format buy?
studies.plain: Lower precision makes each GPU's maths faster but leaves the gradient exchange the same size, so scaling efficiency could drop even as throughput rises. FP8 here uses NVIDIA Transformer Engine, compared with Transformer Engine BF16 so the only change is the number format.
design: H100 only. FP32 (no autocast) and Transformer Engine BF16 versus the default BF16 autocast; FP8 versus Transformer Engine BF16.
GPT-2 8×1024, DistilBERT 32×512, TinyLlama 2×1024 (FP32 memory), 1/2/4 GPUs.
findings: DistilBERT: FP32 is -79%, -78%, -78% vs BF16 (1/2/4 GPUs); FP8 is +4.9%, +4.0%, +2.7% vs TE BF16.
TinyLlama-1.1B: FP32 is -70%, -66%, -66% vs BF16 (1/2/4 GPUs).

Slower arithmetic hides communication: at 4 GPUs FP32 scales better than BF16 (DistilBERT +6.0 pts, GPT-2 +2.4 pts, TinyLlama +10.1 pts of efficiency), yet it is still 56–79% slower in absolute throughput. Faster formats trade a little scaling for a lot of speed.
FP8 versus TE BF16 at 4 GPUs changes efficiency by DistilBERT -2.0 pts, GPT-2 -0.7 pts — the same direction, much smaller.
caveats: No L40S precision runs yet, so the PCIe version of this question is open.

studies.title: Run-length check
studies.question: Are 200 measured updates enough, or does throughput drift over longer runs?
studies.plain: Every deep-dive number comes from 200 measured optimizer updates. This check repeats two conditions for 1,000 updates.
design: H100, 4 GPUs: GPT-2 8×1024 and TinyLlama 4×1024, 200 vs 1,000 measured updates.
findings: Both ratios are within 0.1% of 1.000 and their CIs include 1: 200 updates measure steady-state throughput.

studies.title: Micro-batch versus accumulation at a fixed effective batch
studies.question: With 16 sequences per GPU per update either way, is it better to use bigger micro-batches or more accumulation steps?
studies.plain: Accumulation (S1) helped TinyLlama a lot. This follow-up asks whether the same 16 sequences per update are processed faster as 4 big micro-batches or 16 tiny ones.
design: L40S, TinyLlama 1024-token sequences, effective batch 16 per GPU: micro-batch 1 × 16, 2 × 8, 4 × 4 accumulation steps; 1/2/4/8 GPUs.
Follow-up motivated by observed results (planned 2026-10-21 after E418–E433).
findings: At 8 GPUs, micro-batch 4 × accumulation 4 gives 80,589 tokens/s, +28% over micro-batch 1 × 16 (63,113), for 8.4 GiB more memory per GPU.
Weak scaling from 1 to 8 GPUs keeps 79% (micro-batch 4), 78% (2) and 81% (1) of the single-GPU rate: larger micro-batches are faster but scale slightly less well.

studies.title: TinyLlama: tensor parallel versus independent replicas
studies.question: With a fixed number of GPUs, is it better to split one model copy across them (tensor parallel) or run independent copies?
studies.plain: Tensor parallelism (TP) splits each request's maths across GPUs, which can cut per-request latency but adds communication. Replicas each serve their own requests with no communication. The node's GPU budget is fixed: 8 L40S or 4 H100.
design: Layouts L40S: TP1×8 replicas, TP2×4, TP4×2, TP8. H100: TP1×4, TP2×2, TP4.
Prompt 128 or 1,280 tokens × 1 or 8 concurrent requests; exactly 128 output tokens; BF16; vLLM; 30 measured rounds, 3 trials.
findings: H100, prompt 128, 1 concurrent: fastest TP1 × 4 replicas (171 tok/s, 1.31× the slowest, TP2 × 2 replicas); lowest energy per token TP1 × 4 replicas (3.02 J).
H100, prompt 128, 8 concurrent: fastest TP1 × 4 replicas (1,172 tok/s, 1.25× the slowest, TP4, single engine); lowest energy per token TP1 × 4 replicas (0.56 J).
H100, prompt 1,280, 1 concurrent: fastest TP1 × 4 replicas (167 tok/s, 1.29× the slowest, TP2 × 2 replicas); lowest energy per token TP1 × 4 replicas (3.11 J).
H100, prompt 1,280, 8 concurrent: fastest TP1 × 4 replicas (1,132 tok/s, 1.30× the slowest, TP4, single engine); lowest energy per token TP1 × 4 replicas (0.61 J).
L40S, prompt 128, 1 concurrent: fastest TP1 × 8 replicas (194 tok/s, 1.98× the slowest, TP8, single engine); lowest energy per token TP1 × 8 replicas (3.94 J).
L40S, prompt 128, 8 concurrent: fastest TP1 × 8 replicas (1,530 tok/s, 2.10× the slowest, TP8, single engine); lowest energy per token TP2 × 4 replicas (0.87 J).
L40S, prompt 1,280, 1 concurrent: fastest TP1 × 8 replicas (188 tok/s, 1.93× the slowest, TP8, single engine); lowest energy per token TP1 × 8 replicas (4.28 J).
L40S, prompt 1,280, 8 concurrent: fastest TP1 × 8 replicas (1,474 tok/s, 2.36× the slowest, TP8, single engine); lowest energy per token TP2 × 4 replicas (0.94 J).

studies.title: Qwen2.5-7B: layouts, concurrency and goodput
studies.question: Does the TinyLlama answer hold for a model 7× larger, and how does the best layout change with load?
studies.plain: A 7B model nearly fills one L40S, leaving little memory for each request's working state (KV cache). Splitting it across 2 or 4 GPUs frees that memory. Goodput counts only requests that finish within a latency target.
design: L40S only, 8-GPU budget: TP1×8, TP2×4, TP4×2. Prompt 128 or 1,280 × concurrency 1/2/4/8; 128 output tokens.
Concurrency 2 and 4 are follow-ups motivated by observed results (planned 2026-10-21).
findings: L40S, prompt 128, 8 concurrent: fastest TP2 × 4 replicas (610 tok/s, 1.62× the slowest, TP1 × 8 replicas); lowest energy per token TP4 × 2 replicas (2.03 J).
L40S, prompt 1,280, 1 concurrent: fastest TP2 × 4 replicas (77 tok/s, 1.67× the slowest, TP1 × 8 replicas); lowest energy per token TP2 × 4 replicas (12.07 J).
L40S, prompt 1,280, 2 concurrent: layouts within 0.4% of each other (~154 tok/s); lowest energy per token TP2 × 4 replicas (8.44 J).
L40S, prompt 1,280, 4 concurrent: fastest TP2 × 4 replicas (307 tok/s, 1.09× the slowest, TP4 × 2 replicas); lowest energy per token TP4 × 2 replicas (4.38 J).
L40S, prompt 1,280, 8 concurrent: fastest TP2 × 4 replicas (566 tok/s, 1.54× the slowest, TP1 × 8 replicas); lowest energy per token TP4 × 2 replicas (2.43 J).

Goodput at concurrency 8 (prompt 1,280): TP2 × 4 replicas first meets a 1.80 s target and peaks at 4.4 requests/s (E755); TP4 × 2 replicas first meets a 1.90 s target and peaks at 4.1 requests/s (E758); TP1 × 8 replicas first meets a 2.80 s target and peaks at 2.9 requests/s (E754). Tighter latency targets favour TP2 replicas.

studies.title: Core scaling on H100 (revisited)
studies.question: Do the headline strong/weak-scaling numbers survive the current runtime-cohort selection?
studies.plain: Re-derived from the latest submission cohort per condition. Strong scaling splits a fixed job across more GPUs; weak scaling gives every GPU the same work.
design: H100, BF16 DDP, 1/2/4 GPUs. GPT-2 strong scaling starts at 2 GPUs (the 1-GPU shape OOMs).
findings: Weak scaling at 4 H100 GPUs: DistilBERT 92%, GPT-2 Small 97%, TinyLlama-1.1B 92% — unchanged from the September snapshot.
Strong scaling at 4 GPUs: DistilBERT 73%, GPT-2 Small 94%, TinyLlama-1.1B 63%; splitting a fixed job costs more efficiency than growing it.
caveats: TinyLlama strong scaling (E044–E046) spans two runtime cohorts; treat its efficiency as indicative.

studies.title: Distributed strategies on H100 (revisited)
studies.question: Which way of splitting training across GPUs gives the best speed for the memory it uses?
studies.plain: DDP, FSDP (two modes) and DeepSpeed ZeRO stages 1–3 on the same job. Compare strategies only at the same GPU count.
design: H100, GPT-2 Small and DistilBERT, BF16; all six strategies at 2 GPUs, DDP and FSDP full shard also at 4 GPUs.
findings: GPT-2 Small, 2 GPUs: fastest ZeRO-1 (290,534 tok/s, +19.1% vs DDP); least memory ZeRO-1 (24.5 GiB vs DDP 29.3 GiB).
DistilBERT, 2 GPUs: fastest FSDP grad-op shard (1,279,406 tok/s, +1.8% vs DDP); least memory FSDP full shard (5.6 GiB vs DDP 6.3 GiB).
ZeRO-3 throughput relative to DDP at 2 GPUs: GPT-2 Small 109%, DistilBERT 50% — full parameter sharding is model-dependent at this scale, not uniformly slower.

studies.title: Single-GPU precision (revisited)
studies.question: How much faster is each number format than FP32 on one H100?
studies.plain: FP32, FP16, BF16 and FP8 on one GPU.
design: H100, 1 GPU, GPT-2 Small 16×1024 and DistilBERT 32×512.
findings: GPT-2 Small: FP8 is 3.62× FP32 on one H100.
DistilBERT: FP8 is 5.29× FP32 on one H100.

studies.title: H100 versus L40S on matched single-GPU jobs
studies.question: How much faster and more energy-efficient is the H100 per GPU?
studies.plain: Same job, one GPU each, both platforms.
design: One GPU, BF16, GPT-2 Small and DistilBERT, training and inference.
findings: GPT-2 Small training: H100 is 2.74× L40S throughput, using 0.67× the energy per token.
GPT-2 Small inference (batch 1): H100 is 1.01× L40S throughput, using 1.21× the energy per token.
DistilBERT training: H100 is 2.42× L40S throughput, using 0.67× the energy per token.
DistilBERT inference (batch 1): H100 is 0.88× L40S throughput (energy not measured).

tables.title: Matched pairs
tables.caption: Throughput ratio H100 ÷ L40S; energy ratio H100 ÷ L40S per token (below 1 = H100 uses less energy).

studies.title: Qwen2.5-7B: 4-bit formats versus BF16
studies.question: What do 4-bit model formats cost in quality and buy in speed, memory and energy?
studies.plain: Publisher AWQ and GPTQ 4-bit releases and on-the-fly NF4 against the BF16 model, served with vLLM.
design: H100, 1 GPU, WikiText-2 perplexity; 10% perplexity tolerance.
findings: AWQ 4-bit: throughput +16.0%, memory −63%, energy/token -40.7%, perplexity +7.9% (within the 10% tolerance).
GPTQ 4-bit: throughput +11.0%, memory −63%, energy/token -41.3%, perplexity +4.7% (within the 10% tolerance).
bitsandbytes NF4: throughput -44.5%, memory −62%, energy/token +15.4%, perplexity +6.0% (within the 10% tolerance).
